questions.question: The 'Drain of Wealth' theory, which highlighted the economic exploitation of India under British rule, was prominently advocated by whom?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadabhai Naoroji**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was an Indian political leader, educator, and economist who is famously known as the **'Grand Old Man of India.'**
 
• He introduced the 'Drain of Wealth' theory in his book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India,"** published in 1901.
 
• The theory highlighted how the British systematically drained India's wealth and resources for their economic benefit.
 
• Naoroji was the first Indian to become a member of the British Parliament, where he actively raised concerns about the economic exploitation of India.
 
• The 'Drain of Wealth' theory became a cornerstone for the Indian freedom movement, influencing leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Aspects of the 'Drain of Wealth' Theory:**

 
 
• The theory argued that a significant portion of India's wealth was being transferred to Britain in the form of **home charges** (administrative expenses and pensions).
 
• Export of raw materials and the import of finished goods from Britain created a massive trade imbalance.
 
• Indian taxpayers funded the salaries and pensions of British officials, further depleting the country's resources.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Theory:**
 
 
• The theory exposed the economic exploitation of India under British rule, fueling nationalist sentiments.
 
• It provided a strong economic argument for independence and self-rule.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji's Other Contributions:**
 
 
• He co-founded the **Indian National Congress (INC)** in 1885, which later became the primary political platform for India's independence struggle.
 
• He was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons in 1892 as a Liberal Party candidate.
 
 
 
• **Other Advocates of Economic Nationalism:**
 
 
• While Naoroji introduced the 'Drain of Wealth' theory, other leaders like Gopal Krishna Gokhale and R.C. Dutt also highlighted the economic impact of British policies.

questions.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi travel to Noakhali in 1946?

options.text: To support the Bengal famine victims
To organise the Quit India Movement
To lead a protest against British rule
To promote communal harmony after religious violence

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To promote communal harmony after religious violence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi traveled to Noakhali in 1946 to address the widespread **communal violence** that erupted between Hindus and Muslims in the region.
 
• He undertook a **"peace mission"** to restore harmony and rebuild trust between the communities affected by the riots.
 
• Gandhi adopted the strategy of **walking through the villages** of Noakhali, preaching non-violence and communal unity to the people.
 
• He stayed in the region for several months, undertaking **constructive work** such as promoting mutual understanding, resolving disputes, and advocating for peaceful coexistence.
 
• Noakhali became a symbol of Gandhi's commitment to **non-violence and communal reconciliation**, even in the face of intense societal strife.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Background of Noakhali Riots:**

 
 
• The Noakhali riots occurred in October 1946 in Bengal, marked by communal violence primarily targeted at the Hindu community in Muslim-majority areas.
 
• These riots were part of the larger communal unrest during the pre-Partition period in India, fueled by political and religious tensions.
 
 
 
• **Gandhi's Non-Violent Approach:**
 
 
• Gandhi emphasized the principles of **ahimsa (non-violence)** and **satyagraha (truth force)** to resolve conflicts.
 
• He believed in addressing the root causes of hatred and mistrust through dialogue and personal interaction.
 
 
 
• **Key Activities in Noakhali:**
 
 
• Gandhi conducted **prayer meetings**, encouraged interfaith dialogue, and engaged in relief efforts for victims of the violence.
 
• He advocated for women’s safety and empowerment, as many women were victims of violence during the riots.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Noakhali Mission:**
 
 
• Gandhi’s efforts in Noakhali are remembered as a testament to his unwavering commitment to peace and communal harmony.
 
• It highlighted the importance of grassroots-level engagement in addressing societal conflicts.

questions.question: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent extremist leader, wrote the newspaper 'Mahratta' in which language?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**English**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, a key leader of the Indian independence movement, was a staunch nationalist and one of the pioneers of the extremist faction.
 
• Tilak edited two newspapers: **'Kesari'**, published in Marathi, and **'Mahratta'**, published in English.
 
• The newspaper **'Mahratta'** was founded to promote nationalism and disseminate Tilak's political ideologies among educated Indians.
 
• Through his writings in 'Mahratta', Tilak criticized British policies and advocated for Swaraj (self-rule).
 
• The English-language newspaper was instrumental in reaching a wider audience, including educated Indians and intellectuals across the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:**

 
 
• He was popularly known as **'Lokmanya Tilak'**, meaning 'accepted by the people as their leader.'
 
• He is regarded as the 'Father of Indian Unrest' due to his strong opposition to British rule.
 
• Tilak was one of the first leaders to demand complete independence (Purna Swaraj) for India.
 
• His famous slogan was **"Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it."**
 
 
 
• **'Kesari' and 'Mahratta' Newspapers:**
 
 
• 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English) were used as platforms to spread anti-colonial sentiments.
 
• 'Kesari' was especially influential among the Marathi-speaking population.
 
• Both newspapers played a crucial role in inspiring Indians to fight for independence.
 
 
 
• **Concept of Swaraj:**
 
 
• Swaraj, meaning self-rule, was a central theme of Tilak's political philosophy.
 
• Tilak believed in empowering Indians politically, culturally, and economically to achieve independence.
 
• His ideas laid the foundation for future leaders like Mahatma Gandhi in the struggle for freedom.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak remains one of the most respected and influential leaders of India’s freedom struggle.
 
• His contributions continue to be studied and celebrated in Indian political and historical discourse.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violent incident at Chauri Chaura. In which present-day state is Chauri Chaura located?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Chauri Chaura is a town located in the **Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh**, India.
 
• The **Chauri Chaura incident** occurred on **February 4, 1922**, during the Non-Cooperation Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• This violent event involved the burning of a police station by protestors, resulting in the death of 22 policemen.
 
• Following the incident, Mahatma Gandhi, emphasizing non-violence, called off the **Non-Cooperation Movement**.
 
• The Chauri Chaura event is considered a turning point in India's freedom struggle, showcasing the challenges of maintaining non-violent civil disobedience.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement**: Launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920, it aimed to resist British rule through non-violent means such as boycotting British goods, institutions, and services.
 
• **Significance of Chauri Chaura**: The incident highlighted the difficulties of controlling large-scale movements and maintaining non-violence in mass protests.
 
• **Gorakhpur District**: Known for its historical and cultural significance, Gorakhpur is also the headquarters of the Gorakhnath Math, a prominent religious institution in Uttar Pradesh.
 
• **Impact on Indian Freedom Struggle**: The suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement led to a temporary decline in mass protests but also paved the way for future campaigns like the Civil Disobedience Movement.
 
• **Gandhi's Philosophy of Non-Violence**: The incident reinforced Gandhi's commitment to non-violence (Ahimsa) as the cornerstone of India's independence struggle.

questions.question: In 1820-21, which tribal group led a revolt against the authorities in the area now known as West Singhbhum district of Jharkhand, which was later suppressed by the British?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ho tribes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Ho tribes** are an indigenous tribal group residing primarily in the Chotanagpur Plateau region, including areas of modern-day Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal.
 
• In 1820-21, the Ho tribes led a major revolt against British colonial authorities in what is now the **West Singhbhum district** of Jharkhand.
 
• The revolt was fueled by grievances against British interference in their autonomy and traditional systems, as well as exploitation by moneylenders and landlords.
 
• British forces eventually suppressed the rebellion, but the Ho resistance continued to be a symbol of tribal assertion and defiance against colonial rule.
 
• The Ho uprisings are considered a significant part of India's tribal resistance movements during the 19th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tribal Revolts in India:**

 
 
• Tribal revolts were a series of uprisings by indigenous communities against colonial oppression and exploitation during the British rule.
 
• Examples include the Santhal Rebellion (1855-56), Munda Rebellion (1899-1900), and the Khasi Uprising (1829-1833).
 
 
 
• **West Singhbhum District:**
 
 
• Located in Jharkhand, it is known for its rich mineral resources and dense forests.
 
• The district is home to several tribal communities, including Ho, Santhal, and Munda tribes.
 
 
 
• **Ho Language and Culture:**
 
 
• The Ho people speak the Ho language, which belongs to the Munda family of languages.
 
• They have a rich cultural heritage, including traditional dances, songs, and festivals like Mage Parab.
 
 
 
• **Colonial Exploitation:**
 
 
• The British colonial administration disrupted tribal governance systems and imposed exploitative revenue and forest policies.
 
• Tribal populations also faced exploitation from moneylenders and zamindars, leading to widespread discontent.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Tribal Resistance:**
 
 
• Tribal uprisings played a significant role in shaping the freedom movement by highlighting local resistance to colonial rule.
 
• These movements are remembered for their contribution to India’s struggle for independence and the assertion of indigenous identity.

questions.question: Which Indian freedom fighter was one of the first to openly support Marxist and communist ideologies, and played a pioneering role in the labour movement and the formation of the Communist Party of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**M N Roy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **M N Roy**, originally named Manabendra Nath Bhattacharya, was a prominent Indian revolutionary and political thinker who played a significant role in introducing Marxist and communist ideologies in India.
 
• He co-founded the **Communist Party of India (CPI)** in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, in 1920, making it one of the first communist parties outside the Soviet Union.
 
• Roy actively participated in the international communist movement and was a delegate to the **Comintern (Communist International)**, representing India.
 
• He was a key figure in the Indian labour movement, advocating for workers' rights and the need for organized trade unions to fight against capitalist exploitation.
 
• Roy later became known for his philosophical contributions, particularly his theory of **Radical Humanism**, which sought to reconcile individual freedom with collective social progress.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Communist Party of India (CPI):**

 
 
• Founded in 1925 in Kanpur, the CPI was initially inspired by Marxist-Leninist principles and aimed to overthrow colonial rule through class struggle and revolution.
 
• The party played a significant role in organizing workers, peasants, and trade unions in India during the freedom struggle.
 
 
 
• **Marxism:**
 
 
• An ideology developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels that advocates for a classless society through the abolition of private property and the establishment of collective ownership of the means of production.
 
• It emphasizes the role of the working class (proletariat) in overthrowing capitalist systems.
 
 
 
• **Radical Humanism:**
 
 
• A philosophical framework proposed by M N Roy, focusing on individual freedom, rational thinking, and ethical values in building a progressive society.
 
• It rejected authoritarianism, including both capitalism and dogmatic Marxism, while emphasizing human dignity and self-realization.
 
 
 
• **Comintern (Communist International):**
 
 
• Founded in 1919 by Lenin, it was an international organization that advocated for world communism.
 
• It supported revolutionary movements and communist parties globally, including M N Roy’s efforts to establish the CPI.
 
 
 
• **Labour Movement in India:**
 
 
• The labour movement began in the late 19th century and gained momentum during the early 20th century with the rise of trade unions and worker strikes.
 
• Leaders like M N Roy emphasized the importance of uniting workers to demand fair wages, better working conditions, and social justice.

questions.question: Who was honoured with the title 'Assam Kesari' for his courageous role in the Indian freedom movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ambikagiri Raichoudhury**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ambikagiri Raichoudhury, a prominent Assamese poet, playwright, and nationalist, was honored with the title **'Assam Kesari'**, which translates to the 'Lion of Assam'.
 
• He played a courageous and influential role in India's freedom movement, particularly in mobilizing the people of Assam against British colonial rule.
 
• Ambikagiri was not only a freedom fighter but also a strong advocate of Assamese identity, language, and culture.
 
• He was associated with the **Assam Sahitya Sabha**, a key literary organization in the state, and worked tirelessly to promote Assamese literature and nationalism.
 
• The title 'Assam Kesari' was conferred upon him in recognition of his indomitable spirit and contributions to the Indian independence struggle and Assamese society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Role in Indian Freedom Movement:** Ambikagiri Raichoudhury was actively involved in India's independence struggle, aligning with revolutionary movements and spreading nationalist ideas through his writings and speeches.
 
• **Contributions to Literature:** He is remembered for his significant contributions to Assamese literature, including poetry, plays, and essays that emphasized patriotism and cultural pride.
 
• **Assam Sahitya Sabha:** Ambikagiri was closely associated with Assam Sahitya Sabha and contributed to strengthening Assamese language and literature during a time when regional identities were at risk.
 
• **Legacy:** In his honor, the Assam government has instituted the 'Ambikagiri Raichoudhury Award,' which is given to individuals for their contributions to Assamese literature.
 
• **Title Significance:** 'Assam Kesari' symbolizes his lion-like courage and leadership in mobilizing the people of Assam during the freedom movement and preserving their cultural heritage.

questions.question: What was the main demand of the Home Rule Movement?

options.text: Ban on all western education in India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Self-governance within the British Empire**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Home Rule Movement, initiated by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant, aimed for **self-governance within the British Empire**.
 
• It emerged as a response to the growing dissatisfaction with British colonial rule and the limited political reforms provided under the Indian Councils Act, 1909.
 
• The movement sought to give Indians **greater control over their internal affairs** while remaining under British suzerainty.
 
• The Home Rule Movement gained momentum during World War I, when demands for autonomy became increasingly prominent.
 
• It was instrumental in spreading political awareness and encouraging active participation in India's struggle for independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:** Known as the "Father of Indian Unrest," Tilak was a prominent leader who advocated Swaraj (self-rule).
 
• **Annie Besant:** An Irish theosophist and social reformer who played a key role in popularizing the Home Rule Movement in India.
 
• **Indian Councils Act, 1909:** Also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, it introduced limited reforms but failed to meet the aspirations of Indian nationalists.
 
• **Swaraj:** A term meaning "self-rule" or "self-governance," later adopted as a central concept by Mahatma Gandhi in the Indian independence movement.
 
• **World War I and its impact:** The war created economic hardships and political opportunities for Indians, leading to increased demands for autonomy and self-governance.

questions.question: The Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 is associated with which Indian revolutionary?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aurobindo Ghosh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 was one of the most prominent trials during the Indian independence movement, involving revolutionaries accused of conspiring to overthrow British rule.
 
• Aurobindo Ghosh, a key figure in the Indian freedom struggle, was arrested and tried for his alleged role in the conspiracy.
 
• The case centered around the bomb that was intended to target a British official but instead killed two innocent women in Muzaffarpur.
 
• Aurobindo Ghosh was eventually acquitted due to lack of evidence, but the case marked a turning point in his life as he shifted from active politics to spiritual pursuits.
 
• His defense lawyer, Chittaranjan Das, famously described Aurobindo as "the poet of patriotism" and "the prophet of nationalism."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Aurobindo Ghosh:** Known for his revolutionary activities and later as a spiritual leader, he founded the Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry.
 
• **The Anushilan Samiti:** A secret revolutionary organization involved in the Alipore Bomb Case, aimed at overthrowing British rule through armed struggle.
 
• **Chittaranjan Das:** A prominent lawyer and nationalist leader who defended Aurobindo Ghosh during the trial, highlighting his intellectual and spiritual contributions.
 
• **Impact of the Case:** The Alipore Bomb Case influenced the trajectory of the Indian freedom movement, inspiring many revolutionaries and leading to stricter British surveillance.
 
• **Shift to Spirituality:** After his acquittal, Aurobindo Ghosh moved away from revolutionary politics and focused on spiritual philosophy and integral yoga.

questions.question: ‘Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin’ was written by:
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Rammohan Roy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin** (A Gift to Monotheists) was written by **Rammohan Roy**, one of the key figures in the Indian Renaissance.
 
• The book was written in the year **1804** and primarily aimed at advocating for **monotheism** (the belief in one God) and criticizing the superstitions associated with polytheistic practices.
 
• Rammohan Roy emphasized the need to return to the original teachings of religious texts, which were often distorted by later traditions and rituals.
 
• He is regarded as the **father of modern India** and a pioneer in introducing social, religious, and educational reforms during the 19th century.
 
• The work reflects his profound knowledge of **Islamic theology, Hindu scriptures, and Western philosophy**, which he used as tools to present his arguments.
 
• The book was written in **Persian**, the court language at that time, and included an introduction in **Arabic**, showcasing his linguistic versatility.
 
• Through this work, Rammohan Roy made a significant contribution to the movement against idol worship and the promotion of rationality in religion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sayyid Ahmed Khan**__

 __
 
• **Sayyid Ahmed Khan** was a prominent reformer and educationist who founded the **Aligarh Muslim University**.
 
• He worked to promote modern education among Muslims and is known for his role in the **Aligarh Movement**.
 
 
 
• **Akshay Kumar Dutt**__
 __
 
• **Akshay Kumar Dutt** was a rationalist and a social reformer associated with the **Brahmo Samaj**.
 
• He worked extensively on issues such as **caste discrimination, superstitions, and women's rights**.
 
 
 
• **Keshub Chandra Sen**__
 
 
• **Keshub Chandra Sen** was a leader of the Brahmo Samaj and played a significant role in **spreading its ideals**.
 
• He worked on issues such as **education for women, widow remarriage, and abolition of child marriage**.

questions.question: What was the main issue debated during the 1905 Banaras Session of the INC, right after the announcement of Bengal’s partition?

options.text: Formation of All India Muslim League
Immediate resignation of British administrators in Bengal

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Use of Swadeshi and Boycott**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **1905 Banaras Session** of the Indian National Congress was significant in the context of the **Partition of Bengal**, which was announced by the British in July 1905.
 
• The main issue debated during this session was the **adoption of Swadeshi and Boycott movements** as a response to the partition.
 
• The **Swadeshi movement** aimed at promoting Indian goods while boycotting British products, thereby encouraging self-reliance and economic independence.
 
• **Boycott** included refusal to use British goods, services, and institutions to express dissatisfaction with colonial rule.
 
• The partition of Bengal was viewed as an attempt to divide Indians along **religious lines**, creating discord between Hindus and Muslims.
 
• The session under the leadership of **Gopal Krishna Gokhale** emphasized the importance of **unity and mass mobilization** against British policies.
 
• The Swadeshi and Boycott movements became a cornerstone of the Indian freedom struggle, inspiring future movements against British rule.
 
• It also marked a shift towards a more **assertive stance** by the Congress against British colonialism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Formation of All India Muslim League**__

 __
 
• The **All India Muslim League** was formed later in **1906** in Dhaka, not directly linked to the 1905 Banaras session.
 
• It was established to represent the interests of Muslims in India and eventually played a role in the demand for **Pakistan.**
 
• The league’s formation was influenced by the political atmosphere created by the partition of Bengal but was not debated at the Banaras session.
 
 
 
• **Immediate resignation of British administrators in Bengal**__
 __
 
• There was no direct demand during the session for the **resignation of British administrators**.
 
• The focus was more on **mass mobilization and economic strategies** like Swadeshi and Boycott rather than administrative changes.
 
 
 
• **Demand for Swaraj**__
 
 
• The demand for **Swaraj (self-rule)** became a major goal of the Congress later, especially after the **Calcutta Session of 1906**.
 
• At the Banaras session, the focus was still on immediate resistance to the Partition of Bengal.

questions.question: The Ramoshis who worked for 'Ramoshi Uprising' were night guards protecting the forts of which community?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Marathas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ramoshis** were a tribal community primarily found in the regions of **Maharashtra**.
 
• They were historically known for their role as **night guards** responsible for protecting forts, particularly during the reign of the **Maratha Empire**.

questions.question: Which secret society founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar promoted armed revolution against the British rule?

__
 
• **Abhinav Bharat** was a revolutionary secret society founded by **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar** in 1904.
 
• The organization aimed to overthrow British rule in India through **armed revolution** and militant activities.
 
• It was initially named **Mitra Mela** before being renamed Abhinav Bharat in 1906.
 
• Abhinav Bharat served as a platform for young revolutionaries to engage in nationalist activities, including **training for armed resistance**.
 
• The society drew inspiration from the Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini and his organization, **Young Italy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar:**

• He authored the book **"The First War of Indian Independence"**, highlighting the 1857 revolt.
 
• He advocated the concept of **Hindutva** and was a key figure in shaping nationalist ideology.
 
• Imprisoned in the Cellular Jail (Kalapani) in Andaman and Nicobar Islands for his revolutionary activities.
 
 
 
• **Mitra Mela:**
 
 
• Founded by Savarkar in 1899, it was a precursor to Abhinav Bharat.
 
• Focused on fostering patriotism and organizing youth for revolutionary activities.
 
 
 
• **Giuseppe Mazzini:**
 
 
• An Italian revolutionary whose ideas influenced Savarkar.
 
• Founder of **Young Italy**, an organization advocating for Italian unification and independence.
 
 
 
• **Revolutionary Activities:**

• It laid the groundwork for future revolutionary groups like the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association**.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**

• Savarkar's vision of armed resistance influenced subsequent revolutionary movements in India.

questions.question: Who among the following was a radical rationalist and iconoclast in Maharashtra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gopal Ganesh Agarkar**__.

__
 
• **Gopal Ganesh Agarkar** was a radical rationalist and social reformer from Maharashtra who strongly opposed orthodox traditions and superstitions.
 
• He was a co-founder of the **Deccan Education Society** and the first editor of the Marathi newspaper **‘Kesari’**, later founding his own paper, **‘Sudharak’**, to promote rationalist views.
 
• Agarkar advocated for education, women's rights, and the eradication of caste discrimination in society, aligning with radical reformist ideologies.
 
• He was critical of religious orthodoxy and promoted **scientific temper and rational thinking**, challenging societal norms during the late 19th century.
 
• Despite his close association with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Agarkar held contrasting views on social reform versus political activism, emphasizing social change over political independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Radical Rationalism:**

 
 
• It is a philosophical and social reform approach emphasizing reasoning, evidence-based thinking, and scientific temper.
 
• Radical rationalists often challenge traditional beliefs, superstitions, and practices that lack logical or empirical support.
 
 
 
• **Deccan Education Society:**
 
 
• Founded in 1884 by Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and others, it aimed to provide quality education with a focus on Indian culture and values.
 
• The society established prestigious institutions like Fergusson College in Pune.
 
 
 
• **Sudharak Newspaper:**
 
 
• A Marathi newspaper founded by Agarkar to propagate his ideas on rationalism, social reform, and scientific thinking.
 
• It was instrumental in critiquing orthodox practices and promoting progressive ideologies.
 
 
 
• **Debates with Tilak:**
 
 
• Agarkar and Tilak had ideological differences, with Agarkar focusing on social reform and Tilak on political independence.
 
• These debates highlighted the contrasting priorities within the Indian freedom movement during the late 19th century.

questions.question: The period from 1905 to 1917 is known as the "Extremist Phase" in the Indian National Movement. Which of the following leaders was NOT associated with the extremist ideology during this time?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gopal Krishna Gokhale**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a prominent leader of the **Moderate faction** in the Indian National Movement, advocating gradual reforms and constitutional methods.
 
• He opposed the extremist ideology led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai during the "Extremist Phase" (1905–1917).
 
• Gokhale founded the **Servants of India Society** in 1905 to promote education, social reform, and dialogue with the British government.
 
• Unlike extremists, Gokhale believed in cooperation with the British government and rejected aggressive methods like boycott and swadeshi.
 
• His moderate approach and belief in non-violence inspired future leaders, notably Mahatma Gandhi, who regarded Gokhale as his political mentor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Extremist Leaders (1905-1917):**

 
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak were the three main leaders of the extremist faction, collectively referred to as the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio.
 
• They advocated swadeshi, boycott of British goods, and self-reliance to achieve independence.
 
• Their methods included mass protests, public mobilization, and stronger resistance against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Moderates vs. Extremists:**
 
 
• Moderates, led by leaders like Gokhale, relied on petitions, resolutions, and constitutional reforms.
 
• Extremists adopted a more radical approach, emphasizing direct action and mass participation.
 
• The ideological split became evident during the Surat session of Congress in 1907.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• The Swadeshi Movement was launched in 1905 as a response to the partition of Bengal.
 
• It involved boycotting British goods and promoting indigenous industries.
 
• Extremists played a key role in popularizing swadeshi, while moderates supported it cautiously.
 
 
 
• **Servants of India Society:**
 
 
• Founded by Gokhale in 1905, the society aimed to train Indians in social service and nation-building.
 
• It focused on education, poverty alleviation, and improving governance.
 
• It became a significant platform for nurturing future leaders committed to Gandhian ideals.

questions.question: After the revolt of which year did the British implement measures that reduced the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army and increased the number of European soldiers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1857**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The revolt of 1857, also known as the First War of Independence or Sepoy Mutiny, led to significant changes in British military policies in India.
 
• Post-1857, the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army was systematically reduced while the number of European soldiers increased significantly to prevent future rebellions.
 
• The British reorganized the Indian Army by increasing the ratio of European to Indian soldiers from 1:6 to 1:2 in critical areas.
 
• Key changes included stricter recruitment policies, favoring soldiers from certain regions and communities such as Punjabis and Gurkhas, who were considered more loyal.
 
• The British also positioned European troops in strategically important locations and ensured their control over key artillery units.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• It was triggered by multiple factors, including resentment against British policies, economic exploitation, and the introduction of the Enfield rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat.
 
• The revolt began in Meerut and quickly spread across northern and central India, involving soldiers, peasants, and local rulers.
 
• Prominent leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Tantia Tope, Nana Sahib, and Begum Hazrat Mahal.
 
 
 
• **British Military Reforms Post-1857:**
 
 
• The command structure of the army was centralized under British control.
 
• Significant investments were made in infrastructure, such as railways and telegraphs, to enable rapid troop movement.
 
• European officers were placed in key positions, and Indian soldiers were deliberately kept away from sensitive areas like artillery.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Revolt:**
 
 
• The revolt led to the end of the East India Company's rule, and governance was transferred directly to the British Crown under the Government of India Act 1858.
 
• It also marked a shift in British policies, with a focus on consolidating power and preventing further uprisings.
 
 
 
• **Terminology:**
 
 
• "Sepoy Mutiny" is a term used by British historians, while Indian historians often refer to it as the "First War of Independence."
 
• The term "divide and rule" was implemented more rigorously post-1857 to maintain control by exploiting religious and regional divisions.

questions.question: Which British Viceroy described the Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority' of the Indian population, thereby dismissing its political relevance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Dufferin**__.

__
 
• Lord Dufferin served as the **Viceroy of India from 1884 to 1888**.
 
• He described the Indian National Congress as representing only a **"microscopic minority"** of the Indian population during its early years.
 
• This statement was made in the context of Congress’s first session held in 1885, which was attended by a limited number of elite Indians.
 
• Lord Dufferin's dismissal of Congress indicated the British administration's reluctance to acknowledge its political relevance at that time.
 
• His remarks reflected the colonial mindset that underestimated the growing political aspirations of Indians and paved the way for future nationalist movements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress:**

 
 
• Founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, and others, initially aimed at creating a platform for civic and political dialogue among educated Indians.
 
• Its first session was held in Bombay (now Mumbai) with 72 delegates.
 
• It played a pivotal role in India's freedom struggle and evolved into a mass movement in later years.
 
 
 
• **Lord Dufferin's Era:**
 
 
• His tenure witnessed the establishment of the Indian National Congress.
 
• He introduced reforms in education and public works, but his policies largely aimed at consolidating British authority in India.
 
 
 
• **Colonial Mindset:**
 
 
• The British often dismissed Indian aspirations for self-rule as premature and irrelevant.
 
• Statements like "microscopic minority" reflected the paternalistic attitude of the British administration towards Indian leaders.
 
 
 
• **Congress's Growth:**
 
 
• Despite early dismissals, the Congress steadily grew into a powerful political organization representing diverse sections of Indian society.
 
• By the early 20th century, it became the driving force behind India's independence movement.

questions.question: In which early INC session was the demand first raised for the Indianisation of the higher administrative services, including the civil services?

__
 
• The demand for **Indianisation** of higher administrative services, including the civil services, was first formally raised during the **Bombay Session of the Indian National Congress (INC) in 1885**.
 
• This session marked the **foundation of the INC**, which aimed to voice Indian aspirations and seek reforms from the British administration.
 
• One of the key demands during this session was to ensure **greater representation of Indians in administrative services**, as these services were dominated by British officials, leading to a lack of Indian involvement in decision-making processes.
 
• The demand for Indianisation was rooted in the belief that **Indians were equally competent** to serve in higher administrative roles and that their inclusion would lead to more effective governance.
 
• This issue was significant as it highlighted the growing nationalist sentiment and dissatisfaction with British policies that excluded Indians from key roles in governance.
 
• The Bombay Session was presided over by **W.C. Bonnerjee**, the first president of the INC, and laid the foundation for subsequent sessions to address various political and economic grievances.
 
• The demand for Indianisation of administrative services became a recurring theme in the early years of the INC and reflected the aspirations of educated Indians for equal opportunities under British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Allahabad Session, 1890**__

 __
 
• The Allahabad Session of INC in **1890** was presided over by **Pherozeshah Mehta**.
 
• This session focused on broader issues like **economic reforms and self-governance** but did not specifically raise the demand for Indianisation of administrative services.
 
 
 
• **Calcutta Session, 1886**__
 __
 
• The **Calcutta Session of 1886** was significant as it was presided over by **Dadabhai Naoroji**, one of the founding members of the INC.
 
• Although the session addressed issues related to **economic exploitation by the British**, Indianisation was not the central focus.
 
 
 
• **Madras Session, 1887**__
 
 
• The **Madras Session of 1887** was presided over by **Badruddin Tyabji**, the first Muslim president of the INC.
 
• This session was more focused on **unity and communal harmony** among Indians rather than administrative reforms.

questions.question: At which session of the Indian National Congress was the resolution for Poorna Swaraj (complete independence) passed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lahore Session, 1929**__.

__
 
• The resolution for **Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence)** was passed during the **Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929**.
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru** presided over the session, marking a significant moment in India's freedom struggle.
 
• The declaration of Poorna Swaraj was officially adopted on **26th January 1930**, which was later commemorated as Republic Day after independence.
 
• The session also decided to boycott British goods and institutions to intensify the freedom struggle.
 
• The demand for complete independence replaced the earlier goal of **dominion status**, aligning the Congress with the aspirations of the masses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC):**

 
 
• Founded in 1885, the INC played a pivotal role in India's struggle for independence.
 
• It served as a platform for leaders like Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, and others to mobilize the masses.
 
 
 
• **Poorna Swaraj:**
 
 
• The term means "complete independence" and symbolized the ultimate goal of the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• It rejected any compromise with British rule and demanded self-rule for Indians.
 
 
 
• **26th January:**
 
 
• This date was chosen for the Poorna Swaraj declaration and later became **Republic Day** in 1950 when the Indian Constitution came into effect.
 
 
 
• **Boycott Movement:**
 
 
• The INC decided to boycott British goods, titles, and institutions as part of its strategy to weaken colonial rule.
 
• This was a continuation of the Swadeshi Movement initiated earlier during the partition of Bengal.

questions.question: The Red Shirt Movement, also known as Khudai Khidmatgar, was led by which Indian freedom fighter in the North-West Frontier Province?

• Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as the "Frontier Gandhi," was the leader of the **Red Shirt Movement** (Khudai Khidmatgar) in the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP).
 
• The Khudai Khidmatgar, meaning "Servants of God," was a nonviolent freedom movement primarily advocating for the rights of Pashtuns and opposing British colonial rule.
 
• The Red Shirts were known for their distinctive red-colored uniforms, symbolizing their unity and commitment to the cause.
 
• Under the leadership of Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the movement adopted Gandhian principles of nonviolence (Ahimsa) and worked closely with the Indian National Congress.
 
• The movement played a key role in fostering political awareness and unity among the Pashtun community in the NWFP during India's freedom struggle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan:**

 
 
• Born in 1890 in Utmanzai, NWFP, he was a prominent Indian independence activist and a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• He is known as the "Frontier Gandhi" due to his adoption of Gandhian ideals of nonviolence and civil disobedience.
 
• Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 1987.
 
 
 
• **Red Shirt Movement:**
 
 
• The movement was formed in 1929 and was initially focused on social reforms, such as education, women's rights, and the eradication of oppressive practices.

• **North-West Frontier Province (NWFP):**

• **Nonviolence (Ahimsa):**

questions.question: Who was 'Young Raja' in the context of Khond Uprising in Odisha?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chakra Bisoi**__.

__
 
• **Chakra Bisoi** was a key leader of the Khond Uprising that occurred in Odisha during the British colonial period.
 
• He was referred to as the **'Young Raja'** by the Khond tribal people due to his leadership and resistance against British oppression.
 
• The Khond Uprising (1837-1856) was primarily a tribal resistance movement against British colonial policies, including the suppression of their cultural practices like Meriah sacrifices.
 
• Chakra Bisoi's leadership unified various Khond tribes in their fight against British interference, particularly in the regions of Ghumusar and Kandhamal.
 
• Despite significant resistance, Chakra Bisoi eventually had to retreat, and his fate remains uncertain, symbolizing the tribal people's enduring spirit of resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Khond Uprising (1837-1856):**

 
 
• The Khonds were a tribal community in Odisha known for their unique socio-cultural traditions, including the Meriah system of human sacrifice.
 
• The uprising was a response to British suppression of tribal practices, imposition of land revenue systems, and exploitation by local zamindars and moneylenders.
 
 
 
• **British Policies:**
 
 
• The British outlawed the Meriah sacrifices, which were considered sacred by the Khonds, leading to widespread resentment.
 
• They also introduced zamindari systems, replacing the traditional tribal governance, further alienating the tribal population.
 
 
 
• **Key Outcomes:**
 
 
• The Khond Uprising highlighted the resistance of tribal communities to colonial exploitation and their desire to preserve their cultural identity.
 
• It also exposed the limitations of British administrative policies in understanding and managing tribal societies.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Resistance in India:**
 
 
• Similar tribal uprisings occurred across India, such as the Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) and the Birsa Munda Movement (1899-1900).
 
• These movements played a significant role in India's struggle against colonial rule, often serving as precursors to broader nationalist movements.

questions.question: Under whose administration was the practice of Sati officially abolished in British India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord William Bentinck**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lord William Bentinck was the Governor-General of India from 1828 to 1835.
 
• The practice of Sati, where widows were forced to self-immolate on their husband’s funeral pyre, was officially abolished during his administration in **1829**.
 
• The abolition was enforced through the Bengal Sati Regulation, **Regulation XVII of 1829**, which declared Sati as illegal and punishable by law.
 
• Bentinck took this reform initiative due to advocacy by social reformers like **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, who strongly opposed the practice.
 
• The regulation applied initially to Bengal Presidency and was later extended to other parts of British India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy:**

 
 
• A prominent social reformer who played a key role in advocating for the abolition of Sati.
 
• He argued that Sati had no religious sanction and was opposed to the core teachings of Hindu scriptures.
 
• He is often referred to as the "Father of Modern India" for his reformist efforts.
 
 
 
• **Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829:**
 
 
• It was enacted on December 4, 1829, by Lord William Bentinck.
 
• The regulation declared the practice of Sati as illegal, punishable by the courts, and equivalent to culpable homicide.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Sati Abolition:**
 
 
• The abolition marked a significant step in social reform during British rule in India.
 
• It helped pave the way for future reforms concerning women’s rights and welfare.
 
 
 
• **Lord William Bentinck's Legacy:**
 
 
• Besides abolishing Sati, Bentinck introduced other reforms such as the promotion of Western education and suppression of Thuggee.
 
• He is remembered for his progressive approach toward governance and reform in India.

questions.question: Who is known as the 'Mother of Indian Revolution' for her pioneering role in the early Indian independence movement and for unfurling the first version of the Indian national flag abroad?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madam Bhikaji Cama**__.

__
 
• Madam Bhikaji Cama was a prominent figure in the Indian independence movement and is often referred to as the **'Mother of Indian Revolution.'**
 
• She unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag, known as the "Flag of Indian Independence," in Stuttgart, Germany, on **August 22, 1907**, at the International Socialist Congress.
 
• The flag she raised was co-designed by her and bore the slogan "Vande Mataram," symbolizing India's freedom struggle.
 
• Bhikaji Cama was also a strong advocate for women's rights and equality and worked extensively for India's freedom while in exile in Europe.
 
• Her efforts to internationalize India's independence movement made her a significant figure in the freedom struggle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Flag**

 
 
• The flag unfurled by Bhikaji Cama in 1907 was one of the earliest precursors to the modern Indian Tricolour.
 
• It consisted of green, saffron, and red stripes, with symbols like the crescent moon, sun, and seven stars representing the Saptarishi constellation.
 
• The flag also bore the words "Vande Mataram," symbolizing the spirit of India's freedom struggle.
 
 
 
• **Bhikaji Cama's Exile**
 
 
• She lived in exile in Europe for over three decades, working tirelessly for India's independence.
 
• She collaborated with other revolutionaries, including Shyamji Krishna Varma and Dadabhai Naoroji, to promote India's cause on international platforms.
 
 
 
• **Advocacy for Women's Rights**
 
 
• Bhikaji Cama was a strong advocate for women's education and empowerment, believing that women's liberation was crucial for a free India.
 
• She used her platform to highlight the plight of Indian women and push for gender equality.
 
 
 
• **Legacy**
 
 
• Bhikaji Cama's contributions to India's freedom struggle are commemorated through various memorials and institutions named after her.
 
• She remains an enduring symbol of patriotism and selflessness in Indian history.

questions.question: During the 1886 session of the Indian National Congress in Calcutta, a major demand was raised for simultaneous Indian Civil Service examinations in England and India. Who presided over this session?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During the 1886 session of the Indian National Congress in Calcutta, **Dadabhai Naoroji presided as the President**.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was known as the **Grand Old Man of India** and was one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress.
 
• The major demand raised during this session was for **simultaneous Indian Civil Service examinations** in England and India to ensure equitable opportunities for Indians.
 
• This session marked a significant step in the **early nationalist movement**, focusing on administrative reforms and political empowerment.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was instrumental in highlighting the economic exploitation of India under British rule, famously articulating the **Drain of Wealth theory**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC):**

 
 
• The INC was founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, with the aim of obtaining greater participation for Indians in governance.
 
• It played a pivotal role in India's independence movement against British colonial rule.
 
• The first session of the INC was held in Bombay in December 1885 and was presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji:**
 
 
• He was the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament in 1892, representing the Liberal Party.
 
• He authored the book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"**, which analyzed the economic exploitation of India by the British.
 
• Naoroji was a staunch advocate of Indian self-rule and worked tirelessly to gain support for India's cause in Britain.
 
 
 
• **Indian Civil Service Examinations:**
 
 
• The ICS was the elite civil service under British rule, but exams were initially held only in London, limiting Indian participation.
 
• Demands for simultaneous examinations in India were aimed at increasing accessibility for Indian candidates.
 
 
 
• **Drain of Wealth Theory:**
 
 
• This theory, proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji, highlighted how British policies led to the systematic transfer of India's wealth to Britain.
 
• It laid the foundation for economic arguments against colonial rule and inspired nationalist leaders in their fight for independence.

questions.question: Which of the following sessions of the INC passed a resolution opposing the Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1885 Bombay**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian National Congress (INC) was established in **1885** by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, with the aim of providing a platform for Indians to express their political aspirations.
 
• During the **Bombay session in 1885**, INC passed significant resolutions, including opposing the Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act.
 
• The **Arms Act (1878)** restricted Indians from possessing arms without proper authorization, which was seen as discriminatory.
 
• The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** curtailed the freedom of the Indian-language press, aiming to suppress criticism of British rule.
 
• The opposition to these acts was part of INC's early efforts to address colonial policies that were perceived as unjust and oppressive.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC):**

 
 
• Founded in **1885**, INC aimed to create a platform for Indian political representation and reform under British rule.
 
• The first session was held in Bombay under the presidency of **W.C. Bonnerjee**.
 
• INC was initially moderate in its approach, focusing on constitutional reforms and petitions to the British government.
 
 
 
• **Arms Act of 1878:**
 
 
• This act prohibited Indians from owning firearms without prior license, while Europeans in India were exempt.
 
• It was perceived as a tool to disarm Indians, further consolidating British control.
 
 
 
• **Vernacular Press Act of 1878:**
 
 
• This act targeted non-English newspapers, requiring them to avoid publishing materials critical of the British government.
 
• The act was repealed in **1882** due to widespread opposition and protests.
 
 
 
• **Early INC Resolutions:**
 
 
• In its first few sessions, INC focused on economic issues, administrative reforms, and civil liberties.
 
• Opposition to discriminatory laws like the Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act marked the beginning of organized political resistance in India.

questions.question: What is the title of Sarojini Naidu's first collection of poems, published in 1905?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The Golden Threshold**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Golden Threshold** was the first collection of poems published by **Sarojini Naidu** in the year **1905**.
 
• This collection established Sarojini Naidu as a **significant poet in the Indian literary scene**.
 
• The poems in this collection reflect her **lyrical style**, which was deeply influenced by **Indian themes, culture, and traditions**.
 
• **The Golden Threshold** is named after the residence of Sarojini Naidu in Hyderabad, which was also a hub for **intellectual and political discussions**.
 
• Her work in this collection combines elements of **nature, love, and patriotism**, showcasing her ability to weave rich imagery and metaphors.
 
• This publication was a stepping stone for her to gain recognition as the **‘Nightingale of India’**.
 
• The collection was endorsed by prominent figures like **Edmund Gosse**, a renowned English critic, who admired her poetic talent and helped introduce her work to the Western world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Urvasie**__

 __
 
• **Urvasie** is a character from **Indian mythology**, specifically in the tales of the Apsaras in Hindu texts.
 
• It is not a work of Sarojini Naidu but has been referenced in various Indian texts and poems.
 
• The term "Urvasie" is symbolic of beauty and divine charm.
 
 
 
• **The Captive Lady**__
 __
 
• **The Captive Lady** is not related to Sarojini Naidu’s works.
 
• This title is associated with **Michael Madhusudan Dutt**, a famous Bengali poet, who wrote an epic by this name.
 
• The poem is inspired by the tale of **Prithviraj Chauhan and Sanyogita**.
 
 
 
• **Songs of the Dawn**__
 
 
• This is not a work by Sarojini Naidu.
 
• The term might have been mistaken for her lyrical and poetic style, but **Songs of the Dawn** does not belong to her literary oeuvre.
